prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states that opened the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my preferred configuration. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model of 2011 predicted that interlayer tunnelling flattens the bands at a magic angle, and the 2018 experiments of Jarillo-Herrero and co-workers found correlated insulators and gate-tunable superconductivity close to that angle. The twist angle then became a continuous control parameter for bandwidth and interaction strength, which is conceptually new in condensed-matter physics. The core phenomena have been reproduced in many laboratories with transport, scanning-probe and optical methods and have carried over to other moire systems. A citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the experimentally established correlated and superconducting states makes no claim about the pairing mechanism, so the open microscopic question does not touch what we would be honouring. I did not move after reading the other seven statements, because the arguments against were about attribution and pace, not about whether the discovery is real. Those arguments are weighty, and I now rate the distance between B013 and B001 as smaller than I did in round 1.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. Eva Andrei's early STM and transport evidence for twist-dependent van Hove singularities and flat-band physics is a genuine claim, and a three-name limit means a public statement that she is outside the prize. The field is also only eight years past the experiments, with the pairing mechanism disputed and twist-angle disorder limiting device-to-device comparison. Against this, optical lattice clocks (B001) carry six of eight explicit preferences, a clean two-name credit and an observable, clock accuracy, that is checked by independent comparisons. If the committee weights maturity and clean attribution above conceptual novelty, B001 is the better-supported prize and I would not call that outcome a mistake. My own ranking of B001 was low partly because metrology is outside my field, and I have taken that into account in this round.

responses.point: Kroll invited me to test the 1e-18 claim against the independent comparison record and argued that clock accuracy has no interpretive ambiguity comparable to the open pairing mechanism in twisted graphene.
responses.response: I accept the invitation and the point. The reproduced accuracy and the cross-continent comparisons do make the clock result more robust in the narrow sense you describe, and I cannot name a scientific objection to Katori and Ye as a pair. I do not agree that the pairing mechanism is the right comparison. The B013 citation does not need a mechanism, just as the 2010 graphene prize did not. The correlated insulators and superconducting domes are measured states that many groups reproduce. The remaining difference between us is about weighting. I give more weight to a discovery that changes what we expect from band theory and opens a new platform than to a metrology advance that follows the frequency-comb and single-ion lines already honoured in 2005 and 2012. That is a judgment about conceptual distance, and I do not claim it settles the matter.

responses.point: Lindroth called B013 persuasive as theory plus experiment but said the committee would have to say publicly who it left out, and that the open pairing mechanism bears on timing, whereas the clock has only a pending administrative redefinition.
responses.response: I agree that we must say openly who is left out, and I would want the record to state that Andrei's STM observations preceded the magic-angle prediction and the transport discovery, were real, and fall outside a three-name credit for the prediction and the correlated phases. On timing I would separate two things. The mechanism of superconductivity is follow-up science, whereas the existence and reproducibility of the phases is established. I also take your point that the clock has no open question about what was discovered. That is a real asymmetry in its favour. What the clock does have is the overlap you named yourself, with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and I do not see that as a smaller cost than the overlap of B013 with 2010 and 2016, which I raised in round 1. I would count both overlaps at their actual size and not use one to dismiss the other.

responses.point: Johansson said his hesitation about B013 is maturity, not originality, called the Andrei question more than an allocation detail, and offered to revisit if I or Mehlig could argue that correlated-insulator physics is settled enough.
responses.response: I think the correlated-insulator physics is settled enough for the claim a prize would make. The 2018 states were seen in many devices by several groups and now in other moire materials, and the continuum-model picture of the flat bands is the standard language of the field. The part not settled is why the superconductivity appears, and I would keep that out of the citation. On Andrei I share your discomfort, and I do not think it can be argued away. The most honest position I can offer is that the prize is for the prediction of the magic-angle flat bands and the experimental discovery of the resulting states, and that her earlier work sits upstream of that. If you consider that cut unfair, it is a sound reason to rank B001 above B013, and I would respect it.

responses.point: Mehlig agreed on the Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero trio, asked that Andrei's exclusion be discussed openly, and urged conservative wording about the phase diagram because of twist-angle disorder and sample variability.
responses.response: I agree on both points and have tightened the citation accordingly. It now names the flat-band prediction and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, without any statement about the full phase diagram or the pairing mechanism. You asked in round 1, as the chair's last question also asks of us, what we would do if the Andrei and maturity questions are not resolved. I would not change my preferred configuration because those questions remain open, because they are the known costs of this prize and I accepted them in advance. I would, however, vote for B001 over any topological configuration if B013 cannot be carried.

responses.point: Olsson moved to B001 for cleaner attribution and maturity, while keeping B013 as her first alternative, and said she would reconsider if the committee were comfortable with the Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero core.
responses.response: I am comfortable with that core, and I think it is the most defensible three-name credit that the supplied names allow. Bistritzer and MacDonald wrote the continuum model together, and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the discovery that tested it. A Pearce-style substitution of Andrei for Bistritzer would remove one of the two authors of the prediction, and I do not think a credit for the prediction can survive that. If you are comfortable with the exclusion of Andrei once it is stated openly, then the remaining distance between us is the weight on originality against maturity, and I would be glad to hear whether you still regard B013 as the more original discovery, as you did in your opening ballot.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from B024 to B001 and said that the topological-insulator entries cannot be treated as safe alternatives until the allocation among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Xue and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposers is settled.
responses.response: I agree that the topological line is not a safe fallback, and I have revised my alternatives to reflect it. I keep B004 because its Kane, Molenkamp and Xue trio covers the theory, the HgTe observation and the anomalous Hall realisation, but I accept that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are outside it and that this is as damaging for credit as the Andrei question is for B013. I have moved B001 to the first alternative because it is the candidate I could support if B013 is not carried. I would also resist your chair's implied view that the exclusion questions in B013 and B004 are the same kind of cost. In B013 the three names contain both authors of the prediction and the experimental discoverer of the resulting states, while in B004 the proposers of the HgTe effect are missing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will judge the exclusion of Eva Andrei acceptable once it is stated openly, or will regard the credit as too contested for a three-name prize.
Whether eight years after the 2018 experiments, with the pairing mechanism disputed, is long enough for colleagues who weight maturity heavily.
How much weight the overlap of B013 with the 2010 and 2016 prizes should carry relative to the overlap of B001 with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, since I cannot judge the metrology side with confidence.

Whether six of eight members preferring B001 should affect my vote. I think support counts should not substitute for my own judgment, but I recognise that my view of the metrology priority chronology is incomplete and that colleagues with atomic-physics expertise know it better.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B013 or the alternatives B001 and B004. My documented ties are to Uppsala, Los Alamos and my doctoral supervisor, none of which is connected to Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Katori, Ye, Kane, Molenkamp or Xue. I use dynamical mean-field theory and would consider recusal if B008 were seriously considered, but it is not part of my configuration. Precision metrology is outside my expertise, and I disclose this as a limit on my assessment of B001, not as a conflict.
